channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Targeting immune overactivity in Down syndrome shows promise in phase 2 clinical trial
item.description: In a first-of-its-kind clinical trial, researchers at the Linda Crnic Institute for Down Syndrome (Crnic Institute) at the University of Colorado Anschutz found that a medication targeting immune overactivity in people with Down syndrome reduced underlying inflammation and was associated with improvements in inflammatory skin conditions, while opening new avenues for research on brain health and Alzheimer's disease.

item.title: Acupuncture‑like treatment linked to sustained weight loss in new study
item.description: A form of acupuncture that leaves dissolvable threads under the skin may help people lose weight, a small trial in China suggests.

item.title: Blood test may reveal which lymphoma patients will respond to immunotherapy
item.description: Cornell engineers and Dana-Farber oncologists found that RNA floating in the plasma carries a signature of a lymphoma tumor's surroundings, one that tracked with whether patients were still in remission a year later.

item.title: Milkshake study offers clues to diet's brain effects in young adults
item.description: Results from a Virginia Tech eating trial add to evidence that the developing brain responds differently to foods that have been through industrial processing or contain ingredients not found in a home kitchen.

item.title: Migraine and smoking associated with increased risk of stroke by age 60
item.description: Migraine and smoking were each associated with a higher risk of early stroke in people who had given birth, while participants with both had the highest risk, according to a study published in Neurology. The study defined early stroke as occurring at age 60 or younger.

item.title: Brain changes in women during pregnancy may be key in finding MS cure
item.description: The very thing that worried doctors about women with multiple sclerosis (MS) in pregnancy could be what leads them to a cure. Researcher-clinicians at The Alfred and Monash University conducted a study to understand the nature of decreased brain volume occurring in pregnant women with MS, out of concern that the changes are a sign of disease progression.

item.title: CBD oil offers no behavioral benefit for youths with intellectual disability, new study finds
item.description: Cannabis contains two key compounds that act on the brain: cannabidiol (CBD) and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). Although both interact with the body's endocannabinoid system, the outcomes of consuming them are poles apart. THC is the compound responsible for marijuana's intoxicating high and can sometimes trigger adverse effects, including psychosis. CBD, on the other hand, is associated with potential anxiety-relieving and anti-inflammatory effects. Despite limited evidence that it works, over the last decade, CBD-rich medical cannabis has gained popularity as a treatment for behavioral problems in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

item.title: Video games may reduce rise in presurgery anxiety in children
item.description: A racing video game may seem out of place in the operating room, but it could help with presurgery anxiety. A study by Yale's Department of Anesthesiology published in the Journal of Clinical Anesthesia found that playing a driving-themed video game immediately before surgery may reduce the rise in presurgery anxiety in children ages 4 to 14. The children were undergoing procedures with general anesthesia.

item.title: Boredom is closely related to poor sleep
item.description: We might think that boredom mainly affects us emotionally because it feels bad to be bored. But a new study expands boredom research by looking at sleep quality as an important factor related to boredom, linking it with impacts on our overall health, too.

item.title: Brain model offers new explanation for memory formation and how dementia disrupts it
item.description: A new framework, published in Brain, could reshape researchers' understanding of how the brain creates memories and experiences, and how disruptions in this process may indicate Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.

item.title: Freezing leftovers? Why some foods thaw well but others turn to goo
item.description: Bulk cooking and freezing your leftovers can be a great way to save money—while also reducing food waste and stocking your kitchen with convenient weeknight meals.

item.title: Novel compound eases paralysis and activates nerve repair pathways in multiple sclerosis mouse model
item.description: A new derivative of a natural compound reduced symptoms associated with multiple sclerosis and promoted the central nervous system's regenerative pathways in a mouse model, report researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and collaborators at Keio University and Chiba University in Japan.

item.title: With measles spreading, do you need a booster shot?
item.description: Now that measles is officially back in the U.S., some Americans are asking: Do adults need a booster shot?

item.title: A vaccine for acne? Scientists are working on it
item.description: Acne affects around 85% of adolescents and can persist well into adulthood. For some, this means occasional pimples. For others, it can mean years of painful inflammation, scarring and lost confidence.

item.title: AI-generated hospital discharge summaries earn higher clinical ratings than doctor-written versions
item.description: AI-generated discharge summaries can meet, and in some respects exceed, current standards of care, according to new research led by iCARE (Imperial Clinical Analytics, Research and Evaluation).

item.title: MRI advance could help monitor fatty liver disease by revealing enzyme activity
item.description: Researchers in Japan have, for the first time, visualized the activity of an important liver enzyme in vivo using an MRI-based approach, potentially providing a new way to detect and monitor fatty liver disease. The condition can progress with few obvious warning signs and, in severe cases, can lead to liver inflammation, fibrosis, cirrhosis and liver cancer.

item.title: How poetry can offer a vital, humane response to dementia
item.description: I'm sitting in the lounge of a Midlands nursing home on a hazy September morning. Most of the residents here have dementia and, as in many care and nursing homes, they lack meaningful ways to spend their time.

item.title: Is my child eating enough? Fathers want more support when it comes to young children's eating habits
item.description: Getting young children to eat can be a source of both joy and worry. First-time fathers may feel unsure about how to manage their child's appetite and mealtimes, according to a study led by Ylva Törner Le Priol, a doctoral student at the Department of Food Studies, Nutrition and Dietetics at Uppsala University. The findings, published in PLOS One, point to a need for clearer and more practical support from child health services.

item.title: Silencing a liver gene may prevent brain damage from rare metabolic disease
item.description: What if the path to treating a rare condition that harms the brain goes through the liver? A new study by Duke University School of Medicine researchers is the first to show preclinical success of a liver-targeting treatment of glutaric aciduria type I (GA1).

item.title: When is a risk worth taking? Hunger helps the brain decide
item.description: Researchers have pinpointed a brain circuit in flies that brings together signals about hunger, food cues and danger to determine when animals take risks. The study published in Science Advances and led by Professor Carolina Rezaval and her research team at the University of Birmingham reveals how neural circuits integrate hunger, food cues and danger to guide behavioral choices.

item.title: How a genetic growth brake helps control brain size—and what happens when it fails
item.description: The gene PTEN acts like a molecular brake. It helps maintain balance during brain development, when specific progenitor cells must be present at the right time, in the right place and in the right numbers.

item.title: Wearable patch could help detect silent heart injury after surgery
item.description: Researchers at McMaster University have developed a wearable device that could help detect silent heart injury in the days after surgery, offering a new way to monitor patients after they leave the hospital.

item.title: Extreme heat in UK linked to higher risk of death for people with cardiovascular disease
item.description: A U.K. analysis of health records from more than 60,000 people with cardiovascular disease shows that, over a 16-year period, those exposed to higher long-term mean summer temperatures had a higher risk of death, as did those exposed to more heat waves. Ka Yan Lai of the University of Hong Kong and colleagues present these findings in the open-access journal PLOS Climate.

item.title: People with certain herpes infections have almost 50% higher risk of Alzheimer's or dementia, review finds
item.description: Being infected with herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is associated with a 48% increase in the risk of Alzheimer's disease or other types of dementia, according to a meta-analysis published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases.

item.title: Researchers compare AI tools for analyzing tumor tissue
item.description: Researchers at Skoltech, the University of Sharjah in the United Arab Emirates and Tokai University in Japan, together with colleagues, have published an open-access review of computer vision in histopathology. The review examines how algorithms can identify tissue features in lung, breast, colorectal and prostate cancers.

item.title: An mRNA booster for cellular immunotherapy shows potential against aggressive brain tumors
item.description: A team led by researchers at the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) and the University Medical Center Mannheim (UMM) has developed a new approach to more effectively direct immune cells against glioblastomas. In experimental models, they were able to show that a targeted mRNA vaccine significantly increases the potency of therapeutic immune cells. The paper is published in the journal Cancer Research.

item.title: Lab-grown mini-guts offer a new way to study how the gut renews itself
item.description: Researchers have developed an expandable line of intestinal support cells that can help sustain miniature gut tissues in the laboratory without added growth factors. By making these normally scarce, difficult-to-grow cells available for repeated experiments, the team has created a new tool for studying the environment that maintains intestinal stem cells.

item.title: How your eyes and brain sense the direction of motion
item.description: A ball flying toward your head, a car approaching as you cross the street or—in caveman days—a predator suddenly appearing. To react quickly, your brain needs to instantly know not only that something is moving, but which way it's going.

item.title: Self-adjusting EEG helmet enables easy and reliable brainwave monitoring
item.description: A self-adjusting electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring helmet has been developed to enable easier and more reliable brainwave measurements in various fields, including clinical settings, rehabilitation and brain–computer interfaces (BCIs). The helmet monitors electrode–scalp contact conditions in real time and automatically adjusts electrode positions to maintain stable contact. By reducing measurement variability caused by differences in users' head shapes and hair conditions, the technology is expected to improve the reliability of EEG measurements.

item.title: Dual-targeted CAR T-cell therapy shows promise in patients with treatment-resistant multiple myeloma
item.description: A first-in-human study by Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute investigators found that a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy called TriPRIL reduced or eliminated signs of cancer in 12 of 15 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. TriPRIL—short for trimeric APRIL (a proliferation-inducing ligand)—recognizes two proteins on myeloma cells instead of just one. Researchers published their findings in The Lancet.
